source.title: Why We Sleep
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of Why We Sleep by Matthew Walker (2017). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright.

cards.title: Go to bed and wake up at the same time, weekends included
cards.body:
Walker's most repeated piece of advice is consistency. Your body runs on an internal daily clock, and a regular bedtime and wake time help it know when to make you sleepy and when to make you alert. Sleeping in late at weekends and then rising early on Monday shifts that clock back and forth, a bit like mild jet lag.

A steady schedule is one of the simplest, most widely recommended habits for better sleep. If sleep problems persist despite good habits, see a doctor.
cards.apply_it: Set a fixed wake-up time for the next seven days, including the weekend, and keep to it even after a poor night.

quiz.question: Why does Walker stress a consistent sleep schedule?
options: It helps your internal body clock regulate sleepiness and alertness
It lets you need less sleep
It only matters for children
It replaces the need for darkness
quiz.explanation: Regular timing supports the body's daily rhythm, making sleep easier.

cards.title: Bright light in the morning, dim light in the evening
cards.body:
Light is the main signal that sets your body clock. Walker explains that bright light, and especially the blue-rich light from screens and LEDs, in the evening can delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that helps signal that it's night. That can make it harder to fall asleep.

The flip side is that daylight earlier in the day helps anchor your rhythm. Dimming lights and putting devices away in the hour before bed is a simple, low-cost change.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, dim the lights and put your phone out of reach for the last hour before bed. Tomorrow, get some daylight soon after waking.

quiz.question: How can evening light, including from screens, affect sleep?
options: It makes melatonin work faster
It can delay melatonin and make falling asleep harder
It has no effect
It deepens sleep
quiz.explanation: Light signals daytime to the body clock, pushing back the cues for sleep.

cards.title: Caffeine lingers for hours, and alcohol makes sleep worse, not better
cards.body:
Walker points out that caffeine stays in your system for many hours, so an afternoon coffee can still be acting at bedtime, blocking the build-up of sleepiness even if you manage to drop off.

Alcohol is often mistaken for a sleep aid. It can make you drowsy, but it's a sedative rather than natural sleep: it tends to fragment the night with brief awakenings and reduces REM sleep, the stage linked with dreaming. Cutting back on both, especially later in the day, is mainstream advice.
cards.apply_it: Set a caffeine cut-off around midday for a week and avoid alcohol close to bedtime. Notice how you feel in the mornings.

quiz.question: What does Walker say about alcohol and sleep?
options: It improves sleep quality
It only affects dreams positively
It may cause drowsiness but fragments sleep and reduces REM
It has no effect on sleep
quiz.explanation: Sedation is not the same as healthy sleep; alcohol disrupts its structure.

cards.title: Keep the bedroom cool and dark
cards.body:
To fall asleep, your core body temperature needs to drop a little. Walker explains that a cool bedroom helps that happen, while a warm, stuffy room works against it. A warm bath before bed can also help, because it draws heat to the skin and you cool down afterwards.

Darkness matters too, so blackout curtains or an eye mask can help. If you lie awake for a long time, getting up and doing something calm until you feel sleepy is better than tossing and turning. If insomnia continues, talk to a doctor.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, make your bedroom a little cooler and darker than usual, and move any glowing devices out of sight.

quiz.question: Why does a cool bedroom help sleep?
options: Cold makes you dream more
Warm rooms improve melatonin
Temperature doesn't matter
The body needs to lower its core temperature to fall asleep
quiz.explanation: A drop in core temperature is part of the body's process for falling asleep.

cards.title: Sleep helps lock in what you learned during the day
cards.body:
Walker draws on research showing that sleep plays a role in memory. Sleep before learning seems to help prepare the brain to take in new information, and sleep after learning helps strengthen and store it, so it is less likely to be lost.

This is a strong argument against all-nighters before exams or presentations. Cutting sleep to study more can undercut the very learning you're trying to do. Spreading study over several days, with proper nights in between, tends to work better.
cards.apply_it: If you have something important to learn this week, study it in shorter sessions across several days and protect a full night's sleep before the big day.

quiz.question: What role does sleep play in learning, according to Walker?
options: It helps prepare the brain to learn and strengthens memories afterwards
It erases what you studied
It only matters for physical skills
None, if you study hard enough
quiz.explanation: Sleep supports both taking in new information and consolidating it.
